subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has not had a menstrual period for 13 months. She recalls that for several years her cycles were irregular before stopping entirely. She smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the diagnosis and typical features of this woman's condition?

options.text: Menopause is diagnosed after 6 months of amenorrhea and typically begins around age 40
Menopause results from an increase in the number of ovarian follicles and rising estrogen
Smoking delays the onset of menopause
Menopause is diagnosed after 12 months of amenorrhea, averages age 51 (earlier in smokers), and follows 4-5 years of abnormal cycles
Menopause is caused by a sudden rise in ovarian estrogen production

explanation_correct: Menopause is diagnosed by amenorrhea for 12 months. It results from an age-linked decline in the number of ovarian follicles, with decreased estrogen production. The average age of onset is 51 years and is earlier in people who smoke tobacco. It is usually preceded by 4-5 years of abnormal menstrual cycles, matching this woman's history of irregular cycles before they ceased.

explanation_incorrect.A: Menopause requires 12 months (not 6) of amenorrhea, and the average onset is 51, not 40; onset before 40 suggests primary ovarian insufficiency.
explanation_incorrect.B: Menopause reflects a decline (not an increase) in ovarian follicles and falling (not rising) estrogen.
explanation_incorrect.C: Smoking is associated with an earlier (not delayed) onset of menopause, consistent with this patient's history.
explanation_incorrect.E: Menopause is due to declining, not rising, estrogen production from ovarian follicle depletion.

educationalObjective: Menopause = 12 months of amenorrhea from age-linked ovarian follicle depletion, averaging age 51 (earlier in smokers) after years of irregular cycles.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman has laboratory studies showing markedly elevated FSH, mildly elevated LH, and low estradiol. She has noticed increased facial hair.
question: Which of the following best explains the hormonal profile and the development of hirsutism in this patient?

options.text: Pituitary failure causes low FSH and LH with low estrogen
Loss of negative feedback from estrogen leads to a marked rise in FSH; after menopause, estrone comes from peripheral conversion of androgens, and increased androgens cause hirsutism
Persistently high estrogen stimulates thecal cells to produce excess androgens
The ovarian follicle's continued aromatase activity produces estrone from estrogens
hCG from the pituitary drives LH secretion and androgen production

explanation_correct: In menopause, loss of ovarian follicles causes a marked fall in estrogen, removing negative feedback on the pituitary; this produces a specific, marked rise in FSH (with increased LH but no surge and increased GnRH). After menopause, the main estrogen is estrone derived from peripheral conversion of androgens (in adipose tissue). Increased androgens contribute to hirsutism.

explanation_incorrect.A: Menopause is not pituitary failure; FSH and LH rise (FSH markedly) due to loss of negative feedback, they do not fall.
explanation_incorrect.C: Estrogen is low, not persistently high, in menopause; hirsutism results from increased androgens/peripheral conversion, not high estrogen.
explanation_incorrect.D: After menopause ovarian follicles are depleted and ovarian aromatase activity is minimal; estrone comes from peripheral (adipose) conversion of androgens, not ovarian follicles converting estrogens.
explanation_incorrect.E: hCG is placental, not pituitary, and is not elevated in menopause; the FSH rise is due to loss of estrogen negative feedback.

educationalObjective: Menopause causes low estrogen with a specific marked rise in FSH; postmenopausal estrone arises from peripheral androgen conversion, and increased androgens cause hirsutism.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman reports episodic flushing and sweating, night-time awakening, vaginal dryness, and concerns about bone health. Her physician recognizes a classic cluster of menopausal manifestations.
question: Which of the following mnemonic-based lists correctly captures the common consequences of menopause?

options.text: Hot flashes, Amenorrhea, Vaginal dryness, Osteopenia, Cardiac arrhythmia
Headaches, Anemia, Vaginitis, Osteoarthritis, Somnolence
Hot flashes, Adrenal insufficiency, Vitiligo, Osteopetrosis, Stroke
Hirsutism, Acne, Virilization, Oligomenorrhea, Seborrhea
HAVOCS: Hot flashes (most common), Atrophy of the vagina, Osteoporosis (increased osteoclast activity), Coronary artery disease, Sleep disturbances

explanation_correct: Menopausal consequences are captured by HAVOCS: Hot flashes (the most common symptom), Atrophy of the vagina, Osteoporosis (due to increased osteoclast activity from estrogen deficiency), Coronary artery disease, and Sleep disturbances. This mnemonic organizes the classic clinical features that hormone replacement therapy aims to treat.

explanation_incorrect.A: This is not the HAVOCS mnemonic; menopausal amenorrhea is a diagnostic criterion, and osteopenia/cardiac arrhythmia do not capture the classic clusters.
explanation_incorrect.B: Headaches, anemia, osteoarthritis, and somnolence are not the recognized HAVOCS manifestations of menopause.
explanation_incorrect.C: Adrenal insufficiency, vitiligo, and osteopetrosis are not menopausal consequences; osteoporosis (increased osteoclast activity), not osteopetrosis, occurs.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hirsutism and acne reflect androgen excess, not the HAVOCS mnemonic; although increased androgens can occur after menopause, this is not the standard cluster.

educationalObjective: HAVOCS = Hot flashes (most common), Atrophic vaginitis, Osteoporosis (increased osteoclasts), Coronary artery disease, Sleep disturbances.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman has bothersome hot flashes and vaginal dryness. She asks about hormone replacement therapy. Her physician discusses that HRT alleviates symptoms but carries significant risks that must be weighed.
question: Which of the following best summarizes the major risks associated with hormone replacement therapy?

options.text: Increased risk of breast and endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and thromboembolism
Increased risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic fractures
Decreased risk of breast cancer but increased risk of ovarian cancer only
Increased risk of thyroid cancer and diabetes mellitus
No significant risks; HRT is completely safe for all postmenopausal women

explanation_correct: HRT is used to treat menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes and vaginal atrophy, but it is associated with an increased risk of breast and endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and thromboembolism. These risks mean HRT is used at the lowest effective dose and shortest duration after individual risk assessment.

explanation_incorrect.B: HRT reduces (not increases) osteoporosis and osteoporotic fracture risk; that is one of its potential benefits, not a risk.
explanation_incorrect.C: HRT can increase breast cancer risk (not decrease it) and also raises endometrial cancer risk; the risk profile is broader than ovarian cancer alone.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thyroid cancer and diabetes are not the major HRT-associated risks described; the key risks are breast/endometrial cancer, CVD, stroke, and thromboembolism.
explanation_incorrect.E: HRT is not risk-free; it is associated with several serious adverse outcomes and requires careful patient selection.

educationalObjective: HRT treats menopausal symptoms but increases risk of breast/endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and thromboembolism.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has not menstruated for 14 months and has hot flashes and vaginal dryness. She received chemotherapy and radiation therapy 2 years ago for Hodgkin lymphoma. Laboratory studies show low estradiol and markedly elevated FSH.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Normal menopause
Secondary (pituitary) amenorrhea
Primary ovarian insufficiency (premature ovarian failure)
Polycystic ovary syndrome
Pregnancy

explanation_correct: Menopause before age 40 suggests primary ovarian insufficiency (premature ovarian failure), which may occur in females who have received chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy, as in this patient. The low estradiol with markedly elevated FSH indicates failure at the level of the ovary (loss of negative feedback), distinguishing it from central causes. Normal menopause averages age 51.

explanation_incorrect.A: Normal menopause averages age 51; onset at 34 is premature and suggests primary ovarian insufficiency, especially with a history of gonadotoxic therapy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Secondary (pituitary/hypothalamic) amenorrhea would show low FSH and LH; this patient's markedly elevated FSH points to primary ovarian failure.
explanation_incorrect.D: PCOS typically features oligo/anovulation with normal or mildly elevated androgens and does not explain markedly elevated FSH with low estrogen at age 34 after gonadotoxic therapy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pregnancy would not produce markedly elevated FSH and low estradiol in a 34-year-old with 14 months of amenorrhea and a history of chemotherapy/radiation.

educationalObjective: Menopause before 40 suggests primary ovarian insufficiency, often after chemotherapy/radiation, with low estrogen and markedly elevated FSH.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Physiology: Menopause and hormone replacement therapy

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with 13 months of amenorrhea undergoes hormone testing. Results show estradiol 20 pg/mL, FSH 85 mIU/mL, LH 30 mIU/mL, and an increased GnRH pulse frequency. The clinician notes a hormone that is especially characteristic of the menopausal state.
question: Which hormonal change is most specific for menopause (as opposed to other causes of amenorrhea)?

options.text: Decreased LH
Markedly increased FSH due to loss of estrogen negative feedback
A midcycle-like LH surge
Decreased GnRH
Markedly decreased FSH

explanation_correct: A markedly increased FSH is specific for menopause, reflecting loss of negative feedback on FSH due to decreased estrogen (and inhibin) from ovarian follicle depletion. In menopause LH is increased but shows no midcycle surge, and GnRH is increased (not decreased). The very high FSH with low estrogen distinguishes ovarian failure from central (hypothalamic/pituitary) amenorrhea, where gonadotropins are low.

explanation_incorrect.A: LH is increased, not decreased, in menopause; loss of negative feedback raises both FSH and LH, though FSH rises more dramatically.
explanation_incorrect.C: Menopause shows increased LH without a midcycle LH surge; an LH surge is characteristic of ovulatory midcycle, not the postmenopausal state.
explanation_incorrect.D: GnRH is increased (not decreased) in menopause due to reduced steroid negative feedback and loss of ovarian inhibin.
explanation_incorrect.E: FSH is markedly increased, not decreased, in menopause; low FSH would suggest a central (hypothalamic/pituitary) cause of amenorrhea.

educationalObjective: Menopause is characterized by a specific, marked rise in FSH from loss of estrogen negative feedback; LH rises without a surge and GnRH increases.
